title: Malaria as Potential Aetiology and Treatment Complicating Factor in DLBCL Patient: A Case Report
case_text: A 47-year-old man experienced 2 months of progressive unilateral nasal blockage and recurrent anterior epistaxis. He denied other symptoms such as fever, malaise, weight loss, tinnitus, and diplopia. He was initially diagnosed with a nasal polyp and underwent resection. An initial pathological examination indicated malignancy, and he was referred to our centre. He had a history of 5 repeated falciparum malaria infections within 8 years period during occupational placement in Congo and Papua Island, both of which are malaria-endemic regions. He always received complete treatment for every episode of infection and had not experienced symptoms of malaria for the past 2 years. He lived on Java Island, which is not a malaria-endemic region and where our centre is located. He had no other significant comorbidities, including autoimmune disease and immunodeficiency. Data for previous infection by potential lymphomagenic viruses were not available since examination for these viruses was not available in our region. Upon presentation at our centre, he had a WHO performance status of 0 with an unremarkable physical examination. A repeat biopsy and pathological examination showed CD20 (+), highly proliferative DLBCL (Fig. 1a-c). Contrast CT scan showed a mass on the right maxillary sinus, destroying the posteromedial wall of the maxillary sinus, extending to the nasal cavity, ethmoid sinus, and masticator space, with metastasis to right cervical lymph nodes (Fig. 2a-c). Intracranial spread and distant metastasis were not detected. He was treated with six cycles of R-CHOP every 3 weeks (rituximab 375 mg/m2, cyclophosphamide 750 mg/m2, doxorubicin 50 mg/m2, vincristine 1.4 mg/m2, and prednisone 40 mg/m2 for 5 days) with G-CSF support as needed. He experienced no significant adverse event during chemotherapy. A repeat CT scan was performed 1 month after the completion of chemotherapy, showing a complete response (Fig. 3a-e). One month after CT scan, he experienced shivering, fever, sweating, and a return to normal temperature, which repeated irregularly for roughly 1 week, suggesting malaria. His complete blood count showed haemoglobin of 8 g/dL, haematocrit of 27.6%, leucocyte of 2,000 cells/muL, and platelet count of 10,000 cells/muL. The presence of falciparum malaria was confirmed through immunochromatographic testing of malarial antigen (Plasmotec Malaria-3, Indec Diagnostics, Jakarta, Indonesia). This case was considered a relapse since our centre is not in the malaria-endemic region. He was treated with a fixed drug combination of dihydroartemisinin (40 mg)-piperaquine (320 mg) 4 tablets qd on day 1-3 and primaquine 15 mg qd on day 1 (bodyweight of 61 kg). The patient completed the anti-malarial regimen without any adverse event. He experienced complete symptom resolution, and normalization of complete blood count, with no detected plasmodium on blood smear evaluation.

   - Conclude with the Diagnostic Pivot: the pivotal clinical and confirmatory turning point that established the confirmed diagnosis.

   - The verified ground-truth disease for this patient is: Malaria
   - Disease subtype / specific manifestation: falciparum malaria relapse following chemotherapy for diffuse large B-cell lymphoma
